sections.heading: C2 — Signals, roundabouts, railroads and markings
sections.markdown:
## C2 — Signals, roundabouts, railroads and markings

FACT_ID: sec06-R01 | anchor: A02
A dead signal and a flashing red light both demand a stop-sign style stop, while a flashing yellow light on the same page asks only for cautious movement [A02] [A01].
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0041]

FACT_ID: sec06-R02 | anchor: A01
Pedestrian WALK and DON’T WALK displays overrule the vehicle lights for walkers, so a green vehicle light never releases a pedestrian who faces DON’T WALK. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0040]

FACT_ID: sec06-R03 | anchor: A01
A right turn on red is broadly allowed after stopping, while a left turn on red is allowed only from a one-way street onto a one-way street. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0040]

FACT_ID: sec06-R04 | anchor: A01
A steady red arrow requires stopping and remaining stopped except for the handbook’s allowed turns on red; a flashing red light requires a complete stop, yielding and proceeding only when safe. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0040]

FACT_ID: sec06-R05 | anchor: A01
A steady yellow arrow closes an existing protected turn, while a flashing yellow arrow opens an unprotected left turn that must yield to oncoming traffic holding the green. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0040]

FACT_ID: sec06-R06 | anchor: A02
A flashing yellow light only urges caution and slower movement, while a steady green light grants movement with continued watch for traffic running the red. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0041]

FACT_ID: sec06-R07 | anchor: A02
A green arrow protects the indicated turning movement, while a plain green ball leaves turning traffic unprotected and yielding to oncoming traffic and pedestrians. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0041]

FACT_ID: sec06-R08 | anchor: A03
Drivers approaching a roundabout must yield to vehicles already circulating inside it because circulating traffic holds the right-of-way [A03].
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0042]

FACT_ID: sec06-R09 | anchor: A03
Drivers must never pass or overtake another vehicle once they have entered a single-lane roundabout [A03].
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0042]

FACT_ID: sec06-R10 | anchor: A03
An approaching emergency vehicle is met by exiting the roundabout first and pulling over after, never by stopping inside the circle. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0042]

FACT_ID: sec06-R11 | anchor: A04
Advance warning signs only urge readiness to stop at the crossing ahead, while flashing crossing lights and lowered gates order an actual stop. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0043]

FACT_ID: sec06-R12 | anchor: A04
Flashing-light signals order stopping as soon as the flashing starts, while gates add a barrier that must fully rise with the flashing ended before traffic resumes. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0043]

FACT_ID: sec06-R13 | anchor: A05
White lines divide lanes of traffic moving the same way, while yellow lines divide opposing traffic, so the color alone reveals the traffic pattern. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0044]

FACT_ID: sec06-R14 | anchor: A05
A solid-plus-dashed yellow pair permits passing only from the dashed side, while two solid yellow lines forbid passing from both directions. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0044]

FACT_ID: sec06-R15 | anchor: A05
A stop line marks where vehicles halt for a sign or signal, while a crosswalk marks where pedestrians cross and hold priority over vehicles. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0044]

FACT_ID: sec06-R16 | anchor: A06
Reserved lanes restrict use to the signed vehicle types during posted times, while reversible lanes change their allowed direction of travel by time of day. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0045]

FACT_ID: sec06-R17 | anchor: A06
A shared center lane permits left turns from either direction, while a reversible lane carries through traffic in its currently authorized direction. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0045]

FACT_ID: sec06-R18 | anchor: A06
A flashing yellow X over a reversible lane allows turning movements only, while a steady yellow X orders drivers to vacate the lane as soon as safely possible. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0045]
